standard_text: Understand the formulas for area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve real-world and other mathematical problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between circumference and area of a circle.

progression.narrative:
The whole standard rests on one distinction and two formulas. The distinction is radius versus diameter: the radius reaches from the center to the edge, the diameter goes all the way across, and the diameter is always twice the radius. Confusing the two is the single most common error in this standard, so the progression makes radius ↔ diameter automatic first, alongside squaring a number (because area uses r²). From there the arc splits into the two forward formulas. Circumference, C = 2πr = πd, is a single multiplication. Area, A = πr², adds the squaring step and a second, costlier place for the radius/diameter trap to bite — using a diameter as the radius makes the area four times too big.

Once a student can go forward — a dimension to a circumference, a dimension to an area — the standard reverses the question: given a circumference or an area, work backwards to a radius or diameter. Circumference reverses with one division; area reverses with a division AND a square root, which is why it earns its own step. Then the formulas move into real-world contexts — fencing a garden, covering a pool, rolling a wheel — where the student must also decide WHICH formula the situation calls for. Finally the standard asks for the informal derivation of the relationship between the two: doubling the radius doubles the circumference but quadruples the area, the 'above' move that shows a student reasons about the formulas rather than just plugging into them. The through-line we keep naming: find the radius first, pick the right formula, and remember that area squares while circumference does not.

steps.rationale: The first forward formula, C = 2πr = πd, a single multiplication. It is where the radius-versus-diameter trap first appears: πd uses the diameter, 2πr uses the radius.
The second forward formula, A = πr², adds the squaring step and a second, costlier place for the diameter-as-radius error — using the diameter quadruples the answer.
Reverses circumference with a single division. Students who can go forward must also recover a radius or diameter from a given circumference — without stopping at the diameter.
Reverses area, which needs BOTH a division by π and a square root. It earns its own step because the square root is the move students skip.
The At-proficiency application: the student must choose the right formula for a context (fence = circumference, cover = area) and handle the radius or diameter the story gives.
The Above-proficiency informal derivation: doubling the radius doubles the circumference but quadruples the area, showing the student reasons about the formulas rather than just plugging in.

skills.name: Convert between the radius and diameter of a circle

prerequisite_skill.description: Know that the diameter of a circle is twice the radius and the radius is half the diameter.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is its radius?

skills.i_do_script: The radius reaches from the center of a circle to its edge; the diameter goes all the way across through the center. The diameter is always TWICE the radius, and the radius is always HALF the diameter. Watch: if the diameter is 10, the radius is 10 divided by 2 = 5. If the radius is 7, the diameter is 2 times 7 = 14. Every circle formula is built on the radius, so the first thing I do with any circle is figure out the radius.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats the radius and diameter as the same number, or halves and doubles in the wrong direction
canonical_error.example: Given a diameter of 10, says the radius is 10 (or given a radius of 5, says the diameter is 5)
canonical_error.why: The student has not anchored that d = 2r. The radius is the shorter, half-across measure; the diameter is the full-across measure, exactly double the radius.

skills.item_template: A circle's radius or diameter is given in text; the student finds the other. Short-response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is the radius?
A circle has a radius of 7 in. What is the diameter?
A circle has a diameter of 18 ft. What is the radius?
A circle has a radius of 6 m. What is the diameter?
A circle has a diameter of 25 cm. What is the radius?
A circle has a radius of 3.5 in. What is the diameter?

redirect_script.stop: Wait — which is bigger, the radius or the diameter?
redirect_script.prompt: The diameter goes all the way across, so it is DOUBLE the radius. To get the radius, cut the diameter in half; to get the diameter, double the radius.
redirect_script.praise: You halved the diameter to get the radius — that's the r and d relationship.

vocabulary.definition: The distance from the center of a circle to its edge; half the diameter.
The distance straight across a circle through the center; twice the radius.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle has a diameter of 16 cm. Find the radius.'
Is the radius bigger or smaller than the diameter? By how much?
The radius is half. 16 divided by 2 = 8 cm.
If the student says 32, ask 'did you cut in half or double? The radius is the SHORTER measure.'
Your turn: a circle has a radius of 9 in. Find the diameter.

skills.name: Square a number to evaluate r squared

prerequisite_skill.description: Evaluate a number squared (n²) as n times n, not n times 2.

skills.i_do_script: Squaring a number means multiplying it by ITSELF, not by 2. Watch: 5 squared, written 5², means 5 times 5 = 25 — not 5 times 2 = 10. The little 2 is an exponent; it tells me how many times to use the number as a factor. In the area formula A = πr², the r² means radius times radius, so if the radius is 6, r² = 6 times 6 = 36.

canonical_error.pattern: Doubles the base instead of multiplying it by itself
canonical_error.example: Computes 6² as 12 (6 times 2) instead of 36 (6 times 6)
canonical_error.why: The student reads the exponent 2 as 'multiply by 2.' Squaring means the number is used as a factor twice: n² = n times n.

skills.item_template: A whole or decimal number to square. Short-response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What is 5²?
What is 7²?
What is 10²?
If r = 6, what is r²?
What is 3²?
If r = 2.5, what is r²?

redirect_script.prompt: The exponent 2 means multiply the number by ITSELF: 6² is 6 times 6, not 6 times 2. Write it out as 6 x 6 before you multiply.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied the number by itself — that's squaring.

vocabulary.definition: Multiply a number by itself; n² = n times n.
A small raised number that tells how many times to use the base as a factor.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'r = 8. Find r².'
Does the 2 mean add another 8, double it, or multiply 8 by itself?
Multiply by itself: 8 times 8 = 64.
If the student writes 16, ask 'is that 8 times 8, or 8 times 2? Square means times itself.'
Your turn: r = 9. Find r².

skills.name: Calculate the circumference of a circle given the radius or diameter
skills.i_do_script: Circumference is the distance around a circle. There are two forms of the same formula: C = 2πr if I have the radius, or C = πd if I have the diameter. Watch, radius 5: C = 2π(5) = 10π, about 31.42. If instead I'm given the diameter 10, I use C = πd = π(10) = 10π — the same answer, because that circle's radius is 5. The trap: if I'm handed a DIAMETER of 10 and drop it into 2πr as if it were the radius, I get 20π — double the real circumference.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the diameter in place of the radius in C = 2πr, doubling the circumference
canonical_error.example: Given a diameter of 10, computes 2π(10) = 20π instead of πd = 10π (or 2π(5) = 10π)
canonical_error.why: The student grabs the number in the problem and drops it into 2πr without checking whether it is the radius or the diameter. If a diameter is given, either halve it first or use C = πd.

skills.item_template: A radius or diameter is given in text; the student finds the circumference in terms of π or rounded. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. What is the circumference in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = 2π(5) = 10π. Using the area formula gives 25π; forgetting the 2 gives 5π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is the circumference in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = πd = π(10) = 10π. Treating 10 as the radius gives 20π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 3 ft. What is the circumference? Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2π(3) = 6π ≈ 18.85. Using area πr² gives 28.27.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 14 in. What is the circumference in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = πd = 14π. Doubling the diameter (2π·14) gives 28π.

redirect_script.stop: Is that number the radius or the diameter?
redirect_script.prompt: Check what you were given. If it's the radius, use C = 2πr. If it's the diameter, use C = πd (don't double it). When in doubt, find the radius first.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the formula to what you were given — radius with 2πr, diameter with πd.

vocabulary.definition: The distance all the way around a circle.
The number of times a circle's diameter fits around it, about 3.14.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle has a radius of 6 m. Find the circumference in terms of π.'
Do you have the radius or the diameter? Which form of the formula fits?
Radius, so C = 2πr = 2π(6) = 12π meters (about 37.70).
If a student writes 6π, ask 'did you use 2πr, or just πr? Circumference with a radius needs the 2.'
Your turn: a circle has a diameter of 8 cm. Find the circumference in terms of π.

practice_problems.stem: A circle gives you its radius. Which circumference formula do you use?
A circle has a radius of 5 m. Circumference in terms of π?
A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Circumference in terms of π?
A circle has a radius of 3 ft. Circumference to the nearest hundredth?
practice_problems.notes: Decimal rounding with the full value of π.

practice_problems.stem: Kayla found the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 12 in. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Kayla used the diameter as the radius. With a diameter, use C = πd = π(12) = 12π in. (or halve first: r = 6, 2π(6) = 12π).
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: diameter used as radius, doubling the circumference.

practice_problems.stem: A circle has a diameter of 20 m. Circumference to the nearest hundredth?
A circle's circumference is 16π. Give a radius and a diameter that produce it.
One circle has a radius of 8; another has a diameter of 8. Which has the larger circumference, and how many times larger?
practice_problems.answer: Radius 8 gives 16π; diameter 8 gives 8π. The radius-8 circle is twice as large.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why contrast of r versus d.

activities.title: Which Circumference Form?
materials: Card set of 8 circles described by a radius or a diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card into 'Use C = 2πr' (radius given) or 'Use C = πd' (diameter given).
2. For each card, write the circumference in terms of π.
3. Watch for cards that give a diameter — do NOT double it.
4. Debrief: how did you decide which form to use?

activities.title: Doubled the Diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Read Kayla's circumference for a circle with a diameter of 12.
2. Ask: did she treat 12 as the radius or the diameter?
3. Redo it two ways — with C = πd, and by halving to the radius first.
4. Write the rule for what to do when a diameter is given.

content.error_step: Kayla put the diameter 12 into 2πr as if it were the radius.
content.why: With a diameter, use C = πd = 12π, or halve to r = 6 and use 2π(6) = 12π.

strategy_links.why: The diameter-as-radius error is precise and baitable; find-and-fix with a size check targets it directly.
Thinking aloud 'is this the radius or the diameter, and which form fits?' models the check students skip.
Wrapping a string around a circular lid and measuring makes 'circumference is the distance around' concrete before the formula.

questioning_prompts: Is the number you were given the radius or the diameter?
Which form fits — C = 2πr or C = πd?
Did you remember the 2 in 2πr?
Should the circumference be a little more than 3 times the diameter? Is yours?
How could you check by finding the radius first?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plugs a diameter into 2πr as if it were the radius.
misconception_redirects.say: Check what you were given. If it's the radius, use C = 2πr. If it's the diameter, use C = πd (don't double it). When in doubt, find the radius first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the formula to what you were given — radius with 2πr, diameter with πd.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses πr (forgets the 2) for circumference from a radius.
misconception_redirects.say: Circumference from a radius needs the 2: C = 2πr, not πr. πr would only be half the way around.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the 2 in 2πr — that's the full distance around.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a radius of 10 cm. Circumference in terms of π?
quick_checks.look_for: 20π (2π·10). An answer of 10π means the student forgot the 2 or used πr.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Circumference in terms of π?
quick_checks.look_for: 10π (πd). An answer of 20π means the diameter was used as the radius.

sentence_starters: I was given the ___, so I use C = ___.
The circumference is ___π, which is about ___.

worked_solution.stem: A circle has a radius of 6 m. What is the circumference in terms of π?

steps.annotation: Check first — is 6 a radius or a diameter? It's the radius.
Radius given, so use the 2πr form (keep the 2).
2 x 6 = 12; keep π for the exact answer (≈ 37.70).
A little over 3 times the diameter of 12 — reasonable.

faded_example.stem: A circle has a diameter of 14 in. What is the circumference in terms of π?

steps.annotation: A diameter is given, so use C = πd (don't double it).
Multiply π by the diameter.
Write the circumference as a coefficient times π.
Check: would using 2πr with r = 7 give the same answer?

skills.name: Calculate the area of a circle given the radius or diameter
skills.i_do_script: Area is the space inside a circle, and the formula is A = πr². Two things to watch: I must use the RADIUS, and I must SQUARE it. Watch, radius 4: A = π(4²) = π(16) = 16π, about 50.27 square units. If I'm given a diameter of 8 instead, I first halve it to the radius 4, then square. The two classic mistakes: using the diameter as the radius (π·8² = 64π, four times too big), or forgetting to square (π·4 = 4π).

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the diameter as the radius in A = πr² (making the area four times too big), or forgets to square the radius
canonical_error.example: Given a diameter of 10, computes π(10²) = 100π instead of π(5²) = 25π; or computes π(5) = 5π by not squaring
canonical_error.why: Area depends on the radius SQUARED. Using the diameter squares the wrong length (and squares the error to a factor of four); skipping the exponent drops r² to just r.

skills.item_template: A radius or diameter is given in text; the student finds the area in terms of π or rounded. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 in. What is the area in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: π(5²) = 25π. Forgetting to square gives 5π; using the circumference formula gives 10π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 10 in. What is the area in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: r = 5, π(5²) = 25π. Using 10 as the radius gives 100π, four times too big.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 3 cm. What is the area to the nearest hundredth?
sample_items.distractor_logic: π(3²) = 9π ≈ 28.27. Not squaring gives 3π ≈ 9.42.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 7 m. What is the area in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: π(7²) = 49π. Doubling instead of squaring gives 14π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a diameter of 12 ft. What is the area in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: r = 6, π(6²) = 36π. Using 12 as the radius gives 144π.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 2.5 in. What is the area to the nearest tenth?

redirect_script.stop: Did you use the radius, and did you square it?
redirect_script.prompt: Area is A = πr². First make sure you have the RADIUS (halve the diameter if needed), then SQUARE it before multiplying by π.
redirect_script.praise: You used the radius and squared it — that's A = πr² done right.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space inside a circle, measured in square units.
The radius multiplied by itself, the value the area formula needs.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle has a radius of 4 cm. Find the area in terms of π.'
What is r²? Then what do you multiply by?
r² = 4 times 4 = 16, so A = π(16) = 16π square cm (about 50.27).
If a student writes 8π, ask 'did you square the 4 or double it? r² means 4 times 4.'
Your turn: a circle has a diameter of 12 in. Find the area in terms of π (halve first).

practice_problems.stem: A circle has a radius of 3. What is r²?
A circle has a radius of 5 cm. Area in terms of π?
A circle has a diameter of 10 in. Area in terms of π?
A circle has a radius of 3 cm. Area to the nearest hundredth?
Marcus found the area of a circle with a diameter of 12 ft. Find and fix his mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Marcus used the diameter as the radius. Halve it first: r = 6, so A = π(6²) = 36π sq ft.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: diameter as radius, area four times too big.

practice_problems.stem: A circle has a radius of 7 m. Area in terms of π?
A circle's area is 36π. Give its radius and its diameter.
One circle has a radius of 6; another has a diameter of 6. How many times bigger is the first circle's area?
practice_problems.answer: Radius 6 gives 36π; diameter 6 (r = 3) gives 9π. The first is 4 times bigger.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why; the square makes it 4x, not 2x.

activities.title: Radius or Diameter First?
materials: Card set of 8 circles described by a radius or a diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each card by whether you can square the radius right away or must halve a diameter first.
2. For every card, write r² and then the area in terms of π.
3. Circle any card where using the given number directly would make the area four times too big.
4. Debrief: why does using a diameter as the radius multiply the area by four?

activities.title: Squared the Diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Read Marcus's area for a circle with a diameter of 12.
2. Find the length he squared — was it the radius or the diameter?
3. Redo it: halve to the radius first, then square.
4. Write the two-step rule for area when a diameter is given.

content.worked_problem: Diameter = 12 ft. Marcus wrote A = π(12²) = 144π.
content.error_step: Marcus squared the diameter instead of the radius.
content.why: Halve first: r = 6, so A = π(6²) = 36π. Using the diameter gives four times too much.

strategy_links.why: The diameter-as-radius and forgot-to-square errors are clean single-point mistakes ideal for find-and-fix.
Covering a circle drawn on grid paper with unit squares makes 'area in square units' and the r² growth concrete.
Thinking aloud 'radius first, then square' models the exact order students collapse.

questioning_prompts: Do you have the radius, or do you need to halve a diameter first?
What is r² — did you multiply the radius by itself?
Is the area bigger than the radius? It should be.
What units does area use?
If a diameter were given, what is the first thing you'd do?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses the diameter as the radius, or forgets to square, in A = πr².
misconception_redirects.say: Area is A = πr². First make sure you have the RADIUS (halve the diameter if needed), then SQUARE it before multiplying by π.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the radius and squared it — that's A = πr² done right.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes π x r x 2 instead of π x r².
misconception_redirects.say: r² means the radius times ITSELF, not times 2. Write 6 x 6, not 6 x 2.
misconception_redirects.praise: You squared the radius instead of doubling it.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a radius of 3. Area in terms of π?
quick_checks.look_for: 9π (π·3²). An answer of 6π means the student doubled instead of squaring.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 10. Area in terms of π?
quick_checks.look_for: 25π (r = 5). An answer of 100π means the diameter was used as the radius.

sentence_starters: The radius is ___, so r² = ___ and the area is ___π.
Because a diameter was given, first I ___ to get the radius.

worked_solution.stem: A circle has a radius of 4 cm. What is the area in terms of π?

steps.annotation: Area needs the radius — confirm it's not a diameter.
Square the radius (times itself, not times 2).
Multiply by π; keep π for the exact area.
Bigger than the radius, in square units — reasonable.

faded_example.stem: A circle has a diameter of 12 ft. What is the area in terms of π?

steps.annotation: Halve the diameter to get the radius first.
Square the radius.
Multiply r² by π to get the area.
Check: using 12 as the radius would give 144π — four times too big.

skills.name: Determine the radius or diameter of a circle given its circumference
skills.i_do_script: Here I'm given the circumference and I work backwards to a radius or diameter. I start from C = 2πr. Watch, circumference 14π: 14π = 2πr. The π cancels, and I divide by 2: r = 14/2 = 7. If they want the diameter, it's double: d = 14. Shortcut: since C = πd, the diameter is just the coefficient of π — for 14π, d = 14, and the radius is half. The trap is dividing by π only and calling that the radius — that gives the DIAMETER, not the radius.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the circumference by π and reports that as the radius (it is the diameter), forgetting to also divide by 2
canonical_error.example: For a circumference of 14π, computes 14π/π = 14 and calls 14 the radius, instead of r = 14/2 = 7
canonical_error.why: C = 2πr, so dividing by π leaves 2r, which is the diameter. The radius needs one more step: divide by 2.

skills.item_template: A circumference (in terms of π or a decimal) is given; the student finds the radius or diameter. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a circumference of 14π inches. What is the radius?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 14π = 2πr, r = 7. Dividing by π only gives 14, the diameter.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a circumference of 20π cm. What is the diameter?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = πd, so d = 20. Halving to 10 gives the radius by mistake.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a circumference of 12π ft. What is the radius?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12π = 2πr, r = 6. Reporting 12 gives the diameter.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a circumference of 6π m. What is the diameter?
sample_items.distractor_logic: C = πd, d = 6. Confusing radius and diameter gives 3.

redirect_script.stop: Is that number the radius or the diameter?
redirect_script.prompt: Circumference is 2πr, so dividing by π gives 2r — the DIAMETER. To get the radius, divide by 2 as well. Read the question: does it want the radius or the diameter?
redirect_script.praise: You divided all the way to the radius — dividing by π alone stops at the diameter.

vocabulary.definition: Start from a known circumference or area and find a missing radius or diameter.
The number multiplied by π; for a circumference it equals the diameter.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle has a circumference of 18π cm. Find the radius.'
Which formula connects circumference to the radius? What cancels the π?
C = 2πr, so 18π = 2πr. Divide both sides by 2π: r = 9 cm.
If a student says 18, ask 'is 18 the radius or the diameter? Dividing by π alone leaves 2r.'
Your turn: a circle has a circumference of 10π in. Find the radius.

practice_problems.stem: A circle has a circumference of 8π. What is the diameter?
If 2πr = 12π, what is r?
A circle has a circumference of 14π in. Find the radius.
A circle has a circumference of 20π cm. Find the diameter.
practice_problems.notes: Diameter is the coefficient of π.

practice_problems.stem: Nadia found the radius of a circle with a circumference of 16π cm. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Dividing by π gives the diameter (16). The radius is half: 16π = 2πr, so r = 8 cm.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: stopping at the diameter.

practice_problems.stem: A circle has a circumference of 12π ft. Find the radius.
A circle's circumference is 43.98 cm (using π ≈ 3.14159). Estimate the radius to the nearest whole number.
The radius of one circle equals the diameter of another. The bigger circle's circumference is 20π. Find the smaller circle's circumference.
practice_problems.answer: Bigger: 20π = πd so d = 20, r = 10. The smaller circle's diameter = 10, so its circumference = 10π.

activities.title: Circumference to Its Radius and Diameter
materials: 6 circumference cards and 6 radius/diameter cards, plus 2 decoys
activities.instructions:
1. Match each circumference to the card giving its correct radius and diameter.
2. Two decoy cards report the diameter as if it were the radius — set them aside.
3. To claim a match, show 2πr = C.
4. Debrief: what does dividing the circumference by π alone give you?

activities.title: Stopped at the Diameter
activities.instructions:
1. Read Nadia's radius for a circumference of 16π.
2. Ask: dividing by π leaves 2r — what is that called?
3. Redo it, dividing by 2 as well to reach the radius.
4. Write the rule: dividing a circumference by π gives the ____.

content.worked_problem: Circumference = 16π cm. Nadia wrote 16π ÷ π = 16, so r = 16.
content.error_step: Nadia divided by π only and called the result the radius.
content.why: Dividing by π gives the diameter 16; the radius is half: r = 8.

strategy_links.why: Stopping at the diameter is a single-step error perfect for find-and-fix with a 'radius or diameter?' check.
Thinking aloud 'dividing by π leaves 2r, so I still divide by 2' models the missing step.
Gradual release from the forward formula (S1) to solving it backwards scaffolds the inverse move.

questioning_prompts: Does the question want the radius or the diameter?
What happens to the π when you divide?
After dividing by π, is what's left the radius or the diameter?
How can you check by going forward with 2πr?
What's the shortcut using C = πd?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the circumference by π and calls the result the radius.
misconception_redirects.say: Circumference is 2πr, so dividing by π gives 2r — the DIAMETER. To get the radius, divide by 2 as well. Read the question: does it want the radius or the diameter?
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided all the way to the radius — dividing by π alone stops at the diameter.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student gives the radius when the diameter was asked (or the diameter when the radius was asked).
misconception_redirects.say: Reread the question. The radius is half the diameter — make sure you report the one it asks for.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reported exactly the measure the question asked for.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a circumference of 12π. Radius?
quick_checks.look_for: 6 (12π = 2πr). An answer of 12 is the diameter — the student stopped early.

quick_checks.prompt: A circle has a circumference of 20π. Diameter?
quick_checks.look_for: 20 (C = πd). An answer of 10 confuses the diameter with the radius.

sentence_starters: The circumference is ___π, so 2πr = ___π and r = ___.
Dividing by π gives the ___, so to get the radius I also ___.

worked_solution.stem: A circle has a circumference of 18π cm. What is the radius?

steps.annotation: Start from the circumference formula that uses the radius.
The π cancels, leaving 2r (that's the diameter).
One more step to the radius — don't stop at 18.
Substitute back to confirm.

faded_example.stem: A circle has a circumference of 10π in. What is the radius?

steps.annotation: Set the circumference equal to 2πr.
π cancels; 10 is the diameter.
Divide by 2 to reach the radius.
Check by putting your radius back into 2πr.

skills.name: Determine the radius or diameter of a circle given its area
skills.i_do_script: Given the area, I work backwards to the radius — and this one needs a square ROOT. I start from A = πr². Watch, area 49π: 49π = πr². The π cancels, leaving r² = 49, so r = the square root of 49 = 7. For the diameter, double it: d = 14. The step students skip is the square root — once you reach r² = 49, you are NOT done; the radius is 7, not 49.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the area by π but forgets the square root, reporting r² as the radius
canonical_error.example: For an area of 49π, gets r² = 49 and reports the radius as 49 instead of √49 = 7
canonical_error.why: A = πr², so dividing by π gives r², not r. The radius is the square root of that result — the inverse of the squaring step in the area formula.

skills.item_template: An area (in terms of π or a decimal) is given; the student finds the radius or diameter. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has an area of 49π sq cm. What is the radius?

The result of dividing the area by π; take its square root to find the radius.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle has an area of 36π sq cm. Find the radius.'

activities.title: Undo the Area

content.why: The radius is √64 = 8, not 64. Dividing by π gives r², not r.

skills.name: Solve a real-world problem using circumference or area
skills.i_do_script: Real-world circle problems ask two things: pick the RIGHT formula for the situation, then handle the radius or diameter the story gives. If it's about going AROUND — a fence, a rim, a wheel rolling — that's circumference. If it's about COVERING or filling a surface — a pool cover, a pizza, a watered lawn — that's area. Watch: a garden with radius 9 ft needs a fence, so circumference: C = 2π(9) = 18π ≈ 56.55 ft. A lawn a sprinkler reaches 10 yd out is a covered area: A = π(10²) = 100π ≈ 314.16 sq yd.

canonical_error.pattern: Chooses the wrong formula for the context (area vs circumference), or uses a diameter from the story as if it were the radius
canonical_error.example: For 'fence around a garden with radius 9,' finds the area π(9²) = 81π instead of the circumference 2π(9) = 18π; or for 'a pizza with a diameter of 16 in.' uses 16 as the radius in the area formula
canonical_error.why: The student jumps to a formula without asking whether the situation is about the distance around (circumference) or the space inside (area), and without checking whether the given length is a radius or a diameter.

skills.item_template: A real-world scenario with a radius or diameter; the student picks circumference or area and computes. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A circular garden has a radius of 9 ft. A gardener puts a fence around the edge. How many feet of fencing are needed? Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Around = circumference: 2π(9) ≈ 56.55. Using area gives 254.47.

sample_items.stem: A sprinkler waters a circular region with a radius of 10 yd. What is the area watered, in terms of π?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Covering = area: π(10²) = 100π. Using circumference gives 20π.

sample_items.stem: A pizza has a diameter of 16 in. What is its area? Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: r = 8, π(8²) = 64π ≈ 201.06. Using 16 as the radius gives 804.25.

sample_items.stem: A playground platform has a radius of 3 ft. What is its circumference? Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2π(3) = 6π ≈ 18.85 (matches the spec's playground item).

redirect_script.stop: Is this about the distance around or the space inside?
redirect_script.prompt: A fence, a rim, or a rolling wheel is the distance AROUND — use circumference. A cover, a pizza, or a watered area is the space INSIDE — use area. Then check: did the story give a radius or a diameter?
redirect_script.praise: You matched the formula to the situation and used the right length — that's the whole move.

vocabulary.definition: The distance around a circular object — fencing, trim, a rolling distance.
The surface a circle covers — a cover, a watered lawn, a pizza.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circular garden has a radius of 9 ft. How much fence goes around it? Round to the nearest hundredth.'
Is a fence the distance around or the space inside? Which formula is that?
Around, so circumference: C = 2π(9) = 18π ≈ 56.55 ft.
If a student finds 81π (the area), ask 'does a fence cover the inside, or wrap the edge?'
Your turn: a round tablecloth must cover a table with a radius of 4 ft. Area or circumference? Find it in terms of π.

practice_problems.stem: A wheel rolls one full turn. Is the distance it travels the circle's area or circumference?
A circular rug covers a floor. Do you use area or circumference?
A circular garden has a radius of 9 ft and needs a fence around it. Feet of fencing? Round to the nearest hundredth.
A pizza has a diameter of 16 in. Area to the nearest hundredth?
Priya found how much edging goes around a circular flower bed with a radius of 5 ft. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: 'So she needs about 78.54 ft of edging.'
practice_problems.answer: Edging goes AROUND the bed, so use circumference, not area: C = 2π(5) = 10π ≈ 31.42 ft.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: used area where circumference was needed.

practice_problems.stem: A sprinkler waters a circular area with a radius of 10 yd. Area watered in terms of π?

practice_problems.notes: Same circle, both formulas — forces the area/circumference distinction.

content.worked_problem: Edging around a flower bed with radius 5 ft. Priya wrote A = π(5²) = 25π ≈ 78.54 ft.
content.error_step: Priya used area for something that goes AROUND the bed.
content.why: Edging is the distance around: C = 2π(5) = 10π ≈ 31.42 ft.

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on 'around or inside?' surfaces and settles the formula-choice reasoning before computing.
The wrong-formula error is baitable; find-and-fix with a context check trains the around-vs-inside decision.
Thinking aloud 'this wraps the edge, so circumference' models the situation-to-formula move.

So do you use circumference or area?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the wrong formula for the context, or uses a diameter as the radius.
misconception_redirects.say: A fence, a rim, or a rolling wheel is the distance AROUND — use circumference. A cover, a pizza, or a watered area is the space INSIDE — use area. Then check: did the story give a radius or a diameter?
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the formula to the situation and used the right length — that's the whole move.

quick_checks.prompt: Fencing around a garden with a radius of 5 ft — area or circumference?
quick_checks.look_for: Circumference (2π·5 = 10π ≈ 31.42 ft). Choosing area (25π) signals the wrong formula.

quick_checks.prompt: A pizza has a diameter of 12 in. Area to the nearest hundredth?
quick_checks.look_for: 113.10 sq in. (r = 6, 36π). Using 12 as the radius gives 452.39.

sentence_starters: This is about the ___, so I use ___.
The story gave a ___, so the radius is ___.

worked_solution.stem: A circular garden has a radius of 9 ft and needs a fence around the edge. How much fencing is needed? Round to the nearest hundredth.

steps.annotation: Decide the formula: around means circumference.
Confirm the given length is the radius.
Use 2πr; keep π for now.
Round to the nearest hundredth as asked.

faded_example.stem: A round tablecloth must cover a circular table with a radius of 4 ft. What is the area of the tablecloth, in terms of π?

steps.annotation: Decide the formula: cover means area.
Square the radius.
Multiply r² by π for the area.
Check the units: covering is measured in square feet.

skills.name: Investigate how changing the radius affects circumference and area
skills.i_do_script: This is the 'above' move: reasoning about HOW circumference and area respond when the radius changes. Because circumference is 2πr (radius to the first power), doubling the radius DOUBLES the circumference. Because area is πr² (radius squared), doubling the radius QUADRUPLES the area — it grows by the square of the scale factor. Watch: radius 5 gives area 25π; radius 10 gives area 100π, which is 4 times as big, not 2. Multi-step problems also chain the formulas: a wheel's circumference times the number of rotations gives the distance it rolls.

canonical_error.pattern: Assumes doubling the radius doubles the area (treating area as linear like circumference)
canonical_error.example: Says a radius-10 circle has twice the area of a radius-5 circle (50π), instead of four times (100π vs 25π)
canonical_error.why: The student applies the circumference intuition (double the radius, double the result) to area, but area depends on r², so it scales by the SQUARE of the factor: doubling gives 2² = 4 times.

skills.item_template: A multi-part scenario: compute circumference/area for two radii and compare, or chain circumference with rotations. Multi-part response.

sample_items.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. Part A: area in terms of π? Part B: if the radius doubles to 10 cm, what is the new area, and how many times larger is it?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 25π sq cm. Part B: 100π sq cm; 4 times larger.
sample_items.distractor_logic: π(5²) = 25π; π(10²) = 100π; ratio 4. Answering '2 times' treats area as linear.

sample_items.stem: A bicycle tire has a diameter of 22 in. Part A: circumference to the nearest hundredth? Part B: how far does it travel in 15 full rotations? Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.answer: Part A: 69.12 in. Part B: 1036.73 in.

sample_items.stem: A ring has an outer radius of 8 in. and an inner radius of 5 in. Part A: outer circle area in terms of π? Part B: area of the ring (between the circles)?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 64π sq in. Part B: 39π sq in. (64π − 25π).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Outer 64π, inner 25π, ring 39π. Forgetting to subtract the inner gives 64π.

sample_items.stem: A circle's radius triples from 2 to 6. By what factor does the area grow?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Area scales by the square of the factor: 3² = 9, not 3.

redirect_script.stop: Does doubling the radius double the area, or more?
redirect_script.prompt: Circumference uses r, so it doubles with the radius. Area uses r², so it grows by the SQUARE of the change: double the radius means 2² = 4 times the area. Compute both areas and compare.
redirect_script.praise: You squared the scale factor — that's why doubling the radius quadruples the area.

vocabulary.definition: The number the radius is multiplied by; the area grows by its square.
Explaining a relationship — like why area grows with the square of the radius — with examples rather than a formal proof.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for grade-8 work on the volume and surface area of cylinders, cones, and spheres.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A circle's radius grows from 3 to 6. What happens to the area?'
What is the area at radius 3? At radius 6? How many times bigger?
π(3²) = 9π and π(6²) = 36π. 36π ÷ 9π = 4, so the area quadruples.
If a student says 'it doubles,' ask 'the radius doubled, but area uses r² — what is 2 squared?'
Your turn: a radius goes from 4 to 8. By what factor does the area grow?

practice_problems.stem: A radius doubles. Does the circumference double?
practice_problems.answer: Yes — circumference uses r to the first power.

practice_problems.stem: What is 2 squared?
A radius goes from 5 to 10. Give the area at each and the factor of growth.
A bicycle tire has a diameter of 22 in. How far does it travel in 15 rotations? Round to the nearest hundredth.
Jae compared two circular pools. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Jae wrote: 'Pool A has a radius of 4 m; area = 16π.'
'Pool B has a radius of 8 m — double — so its area is double: 32π.'
practice_problems.answer: Area uses r², so doubling the radius quadruples the area: Pool B is π(8²) = 64π, which is 4 times 16π, not 2 times.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: treating area as linear in the radius.

practice_problems.stem: A ring has an outer radius of 8 in. and an inner radius of 5 in. Area of the ring in terms of π?
Explain why doubling a circle's radius quadruples its area but only doubles its circumference. Use radius 3 → 6.
practice_problems.answer: Circumference 2πr is linear: 6π → 12π (x2). Area πr² squares the radius: 9π → 36π (x4). The exponent 2 in r² is what makes area grow by the square.
practice_problems.notes: Informal derivation in words — the standard's derivation clause.

practice_problems.stem: A radius triples. The new circumference is 30π. Find the original radius and the original area.
practice_problems.answer: New: 30π = 2πr → r = 15; original radius = 15 ÷ 3 = 5; original area = π(5²) = 25π.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse plus scaling — chains several ideas.

activities.title: Double or Quadruple?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jae's claim that doubling the radius doubles the area.
2. Compute each pool's area with A = πr².
3. Find the true ratio of the areas.
4. Write the rule: when the radius is multiplied by a number, the area is multiplied by that number ____.

content.worked_problem: Pool A radius 4 → area 16π. Jae said Pool B (radius 8, double) has double the area, 32π.
content.error_step: Jae doubled the area when the radius doubled.
content.why: Area uses r², so it quadruples: π(8²) = 64π = 4 x 16π.

activities.title: Grow the Radius
materials: Table with columns: radius, circumference (2πr), area (πr²)
activities.instructions:
1. Fill in the circumference and area (in terms of π) for radii 1, 2, 4, and 8.
2. Each time the radius doubles, record how many times the circumference grew and how many times the area grew.
3. Look for the pattern: circumference x __, area x __.
4. Debrief: explain in words why the area grows faster than the circumference.

strategy_links.why: The double-vs-quadruple error is precise; find-and-fix with a computed ratio makes the square relationship undeniable.
A journal entry on why area grows by the square of the radius consolidates the informal derivation the standard asks for.
Think-pair-share lets students articulate and test the 'area grows faster' claim before generalizing it.

questioning_prompts: The radius doubled — does the area double, or more?
What is the scale factor squared?
What is the area at each radius? What's the ratio?

Can you explain in words why area grows faster than circumference?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says doubling the radius doubles the area.
misconception_redirects.say: Circumference uses r, so it doubles with the radius. Area uses r², so it grows by the SQUARE of the change: double the radius means 2² = 4 times the area. Compute both areas and compare.
misconception_redirects.praise: You squared the scale factor — that's why doubling the radius quadruples the area.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds a ring's outer area but forgets to subtract the inner circle.

quick_checks.look_for: 4 times (9π → 36π). An answer of 2 treats area as linear.

quick_checks.look_for: 50π (10π x 5). Adding instead of multiplying signals a chaining error.

Circumference grows by ___, but area grows by ___ because it uses r².

worked_solution.answer: It quadruples: 25π → 100π sq cm (4 times larger)

steps.annotation: Area at the first radius.
Area at the doubled radius — square 10, don't double 25.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5 (a real-world circle problem) -- the At-proficiency workhorse where the student must choose circumference or area. If they pass, push to S6 (investigate how changing the radius affects circumference and area). If they fail, drop to S1 and S2 to check whether computing circumference and area from a radius or diameter is solid. S3 and S4 (working backwards from a circumference or an area) branch off as the reversal contexts.
